parts.title: On art and artists
parts.article:
(A) There really is no such thing as art, only artists. Once these were people who took coloured earth and roughed out the forms of a bison on the wall of a cave; today some buy their paints, and others design posters for hoardings; they did and do many other things. There is no harm in calling all these activities art as long as we keep in mind that such a word may mean very different things in different times and places, and as long as we realize that Art with a capital A has no existence: it has become something of an obsession. You may crush an artist by telling him that what he has just done may be quite good in its own way, only it is not true art.

(B) Actually, I do not think that there are any wrong reasons for liking a statue or a picture. We may like a painting of a village scene because it reminds us of home. There is nothing wrong with that. All of us, when we see a painting, are bound to be reminded of a hundred-and-one things which influence our likes and dislikes. As long as these memories help us to enjoy what we see, we need not worry.

(C) It is only when some irrelevant memory makes us prejudiced, when we instinctively turn away from a magnificent picture of an alpine scene because we dislike climbing, that we should search our mind for the reason for the aversion which spoils a pleasure we might otherwise have had. There are wrong reasons for disliking a work of art.

(D) Most people like to see in pictures what they would also like to see in reality. This is quite a natural preference. We all like beauty in nature, and are grateful to the artists who have preserved it in their works. Nor would these artists themselves have rebuffed us for our taste. When the great Flemish painter Rubens made a drawing of his young son, he was surely proud of his good looks, and wanted us, too, to delight in the child's appearance. But this bias for the pretty and engaging subject is apt to become a stumbling block if it leads us to reject works which represent a less appealing subject.

(E) The great German painter Dürer certainly drew his mother with as much devotion and love as Rubens felt for his child. His truthful study of old age may give us a shock which makes us turn away from it - and yet, if we fight against that first reaction we may be richly rewarded. For Dürer's drawing in its tremendous sincerity is a great work. The beauty of a picture does not really lie in the beauty of its subject matter. The trouble about beauty is that tastes and standards of what is beautiful vary so much.

(F) What is true of beauty is also true of facial expression. In fact, it is often the expression of a figure in the painting which makes us like or loathe the work. Some people like an expression - perhaps of suffering or of compassion - which they can readily understand, and which therefore moves them profoundly. But we should not, for that reason, turn away from works whose expression is perhaps less easy to understand. Often we must first learn to know the artist's methods of drawing to understand the feelings he or she wishes to portray, and may even come to prefer works of art in which expression is not obvious. Just as some of us would rather people use few words and gestures and leave something to be guessed, so some of us would rather look at paintings or sculptures which are open to interpretation.

(G) But here newcomers to art are often brought up against another difficulty. They want to admire the artist's skill in representing the things they see. What they like best are paintings which 'look real'. This is an important consideration, and the patience and skill which go into the faithful rendering of the visible world are indeed to be admired. Great artists of the past have devoted much labour to works in which every tiny detail is carefully recorded. Dürer's watercolour study of a hare is one of the most famous examples of this loving patience. But who would say that Rembrandt's drawing of an elephant is necessarily less good because it shows fewer details? Indeed Rembrandt gave us the feel of the elephant's wrinkly skin with just a few lines of his chalk.

(H) If we find fault with the accuracy of a picture, we must remember that artists may have their reasons for changing the appearance of what they see. We should also never condemn a work for being incorrectly drawn unless we are quite sure that we are right and the painter is wrong. We have a curious habit of thinking that nature must always look like the pictures we are accustomed to. For generations, paintings showed horses galloping with outstretched legs in full flight through the air, and we came to believe that this was indeed how they moved. It was only the development of photography which proved that horses simply do not gallop in that way. And yet, when painters began to apply this new discovery, and painted horses moving as they actually do, everyone complained that their pictures looked wrong.

reference:
Q27

干扰 你可能会去其他段落找具体的语言或画作名字，但这里的核心是找到“language”（words/gestures）和“art”（paintings/sculptures）被放在一起作抽象对比的地方。

句子 F段：Just as some of us would rather people use few words and gestures and leave something to be guessed, so some of us would rather look at paintings or sculptures which are open to interpretation.

解析 F段结尾直接用“正如有人喜欢少说话多让人猜一样，也有人喜欢看留有解读空间的画作”，完美对应了语言偏好和艺术偏好的类比比较。

Q28

解析 H段解释了人们因为世世代代看错误的马匹奔跑画作，从而误以为马就是那样跑的，完全符合“误解某种动物的运动方式”。

干扰 你可能会因为题干只提到了笼统的“a certain animal”而不敢确定，但只要看到原文对“horses”和“how they moved”的错误认知的详细说明，就应该果断选H。

句子 H段：We have a curious habit of thinking that nature must always look like the pictures we are accustomed to. For generations, paintings showed horses galloping with outstretched legs in full flight through the air, and we came to believe that this was indeed how they moved. It was only the development of photography which proved that horses simply do not gallop in that way.

Q29

解析 G段把丢勒画兔子用的“耐心细致记录每个细节”和伦勃朗画大象用的“寥寥几笔线条抓感觉”进行了明确的技法（techniques）对比。

干扰 你可能会在E段看到丢勒画母亲和鲁本斯画儿子的对比，但那里比的是画画时的“情感和题材”，G段才是真正对比具体的绘画细节和线条技法。

句子 G段：Great artists of the past have devoted much labour to works in which every tiny detail is carefully recorded. Dürer's watercolour study of a hare is one of the most famous examples of this loving patience. But who would say that Rembrandt's drawing of an elephant is necessarily less good because it shows fewer details? Indeed Rembrandt gave us the feel of the elephant's wrinkly skin with just a few lines of his chalk.

Q30

句子 A段：There is no harm in calling all these activities art as long as we keep in mind that such a word may mean very different things in different times and places, and as long as we realize that Art with a capital A has no existence: it has become something of an obsession. You may crush an artist by telling him that what he has just done may be quite good in its own way, only it is not true art.

解析 A段结尾明确指出，如果你用所谓“真正的艺术”这个词去评判别人，可能会毁掉（crush）一个艺术家，这就是术语带来的负面影响。

干扰 你可能会觉得A段前半部分只是在探讨艺术的定义，但只有紧盯最后一句的“crush an artist”，才能找出题干要求的“negative effect”。

Q31

解析 文中明确提到鲁本斯画他儿子时，也希望我们（wanted us, too）去喜爱这孩子的外貌，这就对应了希望我们“分享他对这个对象的欣赏”。

干扰 你可能觉得这段重点是讲大众审美，但遇到具名画家和画作对象时，要精准锁定“wanted us, too”这种表达意图的关联词。

句子 D段：When the great Flemish painter Rubens made a drawing of his young son, he was surely proud of his good looks, and wanted us, too, to delight in the child's appearance.

Q32

解析 画大象时细节更少（fewer details），只用几条线就给出了大象皮的“感觉”（feel），这就叫给出整体印象而非细节。

干扰 你可能错选成画野兔的E选项，但野兔是细节极度丰富的代表，大象才是“寥寥几笔出印象”的正确对应。

句子 G段：But who would say that Rembrandt's drawing of an elephant is necessarily less good because it shows fewer details? Indeed Rembrandt gave us the feel of the elephant's wrinkly skin with just a few lines of his chalk.

Q33

解析 文中说因为自己“不喜欢爬山”而去本能排斥一幅极好的高山风景画（alpine scene），这就对应了“个人经历导致觉得这幅画令人不快（unpleasant）”。

干扰 你可能会想选村庄风景（village scene），但村庄风景在B段是引发“好感”的个人经历例子，高山风景才是引发“反感”的例子。

句子 C段：It is only when some irrelevant memory makes us prejudiced, when we instinctively turn away from a magnificent picture of an alpine scene because we dislike climbing, that we should search our mind for the reason for the aversion which spoils a pleasure we might otherwise have had.

Q34

干扰 你可能看到这道题会想去找比较抽象的画作对象，但文中提到“factually wrong”并且被科学（摄影）打脸的具体对象只有马（horses）。

句子 H段：For generations, paintings showed horses galloping with outstretched legs in full flight through the air, and we came to believe that this was indeed how they moved. It was only the development of photography which proved that horses simply do not gallop in that way.

解析 过去画马总是画成四腿伸展腾空，后来摄影术证明马根本不是那样跑的，完全对应“曾经的描绘方式在事实上是错误的”。

Q35

解析 丢勒的野兔水彩画是“认真记录下每一个微小细节”且“倾注耐心与心血”的最著名例子，对应“为创造极其准确的画作而付出的努力”。

干扰 你可能会把大象和野兔的特点记混，一定要牢记大象是细节少、抓感觉，野兔才是花费巨大劳动（much labour）死磕细节的代表。

句子 G段：Great artists of the past have devoted much labour to works in which every tiny detail is carefully recorded. Dürer's watercolour study of a hare is one of the most famous examples of this loving patience.

Q36

解析 喜欢村庄风景画是因为它“让我们想起了家（reminds us of home）”，这个“想起家”就是画作本身的外部原因。

干扰 你可能会觉得所有画都有外部情感原因，但文中明确拿来作为“外部情感联想”的具体例子，只有村庄的景色（village scene）。

句子 B段：We may like a painting of a village scene because it reminds us of home. There is nothing wrong with that.

Q37

句子 E段：The great German painter Dürer certainly drew his mother with as much devotion and love as Rubens felt for his child. His truthful study of old age may give us a shock which makes us turn away from it - and yet, if we fight against that first reaction we may be richly rewarded.

解析 题干中的“representation of her age”直接对应原文对她老态的“study of old age”，修饰这个词的形容词正是“truthful”（真实的）。

干扰 你可能会因为看到上一句的“devotion”而想填，但空格后面跟的是“呈现/刻画（representation）”，只能用原文直接修饰这幅画作刻画风格的形容词“truthful”。

Q38

解析 题干说需要克服“initial reaction of (最初的...反应)”，对应原文中抗拒那幅画产生的“give us a shock”和紧接着的“fight against that first reaction”。

干扰 你可能会想填“first”，但题干已经有了“initial reaction”，填“first”就重复了，真正让你产生第一反应并转身避开的那个情绪名词是“shock”。

句子 E段：His truthful study of old age may give us a shock which makes us turn away from it - and yet, if we fight against that first reaction we may be richly rewarded.

Q39

解析 题干中的“without much effort”完美同义替换了原文的“readily”（轻易地），所以他们轻易能对这种表情做出的动作就是“understand”（理解）。

干扰 你可能会被破折号里的“suffering”或“compassion”干扰，但这俩只是表情的具体种类，句子真正的谓语动作是人们能够轻易地“understand”。

句子 F段：Some people like an expression - perhaps of suffering or of compassion - which they can readily understand, and which therefore moves them profoundly.

Q40

解析 题干说其他人更偏爱需要（require）什么的表情，对应原文最后一句，这些人更愿意看留有空间、开放给人们去“interpretation”（解读）的画作。

干扰 你可能会去前一句找“guess”之类的词，但空前是“require”，要填名词，原文最后最精准概括这个行为的核心名词就是“interpretation”。

句子 F段：Just as some of us would rather people use few words and gestures and leave something to be guessed, so some of us would rather look at paintings or sculptures which are open to interpretation.
